statement: In people on a stable once-daily methadone dose in an Australian public programme (18 people studied over one 24-hour dosing interval, published 1999), the 9 who reported regular withdrawal before their next dose, compared with the 9 who did not, had a similar methadone level just before the dose (257 against 249 ng/mL) and similar overall exposure, but their level fell faster after the daily peak: fastest fall 74.5 against 47.6 ng/mL per hour, a difference that was not significant in all 18 (P = .09); the paper reports it as significant after 2 people whose urine showed other opioids were left out, but the editors' recalculation gives a two-sided P of about .054. On average, withdrawal symptoms were fewest in the hours after the dose and rose as methadone levels fell, and people whose levels fell fastest reported more withdrawal symptoms (r = 0.60). The groups were formed by self-report, and the study tested no change in treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of people on methadone, those who felt withdrawal before their next dose had about the same methadone level as others just before the dose, but their level dropped faster after its daily high point. Only 18 people were tested for one day, and the difference was clear only after two people were left out.
population: People on stable once-daily methadone maintenance in the South Australian public programme (in treatment 6 months to 10 years): 9 who reported regular withdrawal between doses and 9 who did not
exposure: Pattern of plasma methadone over the dosing interval, in particular the fastest hourly fall after the peak
comparator: People on methadone who did not report withdrawal between doses
outcome: Self-reported withdrawal between doses (group) and number of withdrawal symptoms over the interval
magnitude: Level before the dose 257 against 249 ng/mL (P > .05); AUC 8.2 ± 3.9 against 7.4 ± 5.0 mg·h/L (P > .05); fastest fall 74.5 ± 40.4 against 47.6 ± 21.3 ng/mL/h, t = 1.77, P = .09; without 2 people with other opioids in urine 74.5 against 42.1, t = 2.10, stated P < .05 (two-sided P about .054 on 14 degrees of freedom, editors' calculation); correlation of the fastest fall with withdrawal symptoms r = 0.60 (n = 18), r = 0.67 (n = 16).

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity in holders and nonholders, 1st paragraph (p. 690); Figure 2 (p. 689)
evidence.extracted: Withdrawal significantly higher in nonholders and strongly inversely related to plasma methadone in both groups; plasma methadone before the dose 249 ng/mL in holders and 257 ng/mL in nonholders (P > .05); peak-to-trough ratio 1.9 and 1.7 (P > .05); AUC 7.4 and 8.2 mg·h/L (P > .05).

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity in holders and nonholders, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 and legend
evidence.extracted: Fastest hourly fall in plasma methadone 47.6 ± 21.3 ng/mL/h in holders against 74.5 ± 40.4 in nonholders, t = 1.77, P = .09; without the two people with other opioids in urine 42.1 ± 20.8 against 74.5 ± 40.4, t = 2.10, stated P < .05; correlation of the fastest fall with the mean number of withdrawal symptoms from peak to trough r = 0.60 in all 18 (P < .01) and r = 0.67 without the two. By editors' calculation the two-sided P for t = 2.10 on 14 degrees of freedom is .054.

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic responses › Subjective responses (p. 689); Figure 1 (p. 688)
evidence.extracted: Withdrawal symptoms were significantly more frequent in the patients than in the drug-free controls at all times and least severe in the hours after the dose; the MBG positive-effect score peaked a few hours after the dose and returned to baseline later in the interval.

evidence.locator: Results › Plasma concentration-effect relationships, 1st paragraph (p. 690); Table I (p. 691)
evidence.extracted: Slope factor N for withdrawal 5.4 ± 0.9 (model fitted in 9 of 18) and for MBG 5.1 ± 1.05, against 1.2 ± 0.1 for pupil diameter: very steep concentration-effect relationships for withdrawal and positive effects; no significant difference between holders and nonholders (P > .05).

evidence.locator: Methods › Patients and control subjects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Nine self-reported holders and nine self-reported nonholders volunteered from the South Australian Public Methadone Maintenance Program (in treatment 6 months to 10 years, no dose change for at least 2 months); 11 men and 7 women aged 21 to 45; urine positive for cannabinoids in 10 and for other opioids in 2; 10 drug-free controls.
In the authors' earlier survey in the same programme, 34% of 114 non-selected patients regularly had withdrawal between doses and 66% did not; plasma methadone was not measured there.

The authors caution that methadone is a mixture of two mirror-image forms whose different handling can create apparent distribution effects, so a distribution (disposition) mechanism for the holder-nonholder difference should be invoked with extreme caution; analysis of the active form was under way.

risk_of_bias.note: Groups formed by self-report; the key difference significant only after a post hoc exclusion; the abstract reports only the subset; several P values do not match their test statistics (card sc_dyer_1999, ROBINS-E high).

indirectness.note: Worded for people on stable methadone in this programme.

imprecision.note: 9 people per group; the group difference has a P between .05 and .10.

grade.reasoning: Observational, so it starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The within-person link between falling levels and withdrawal (r = 0.60 in all 18) is firmer than the holder-nonholder difference in the rate of fall. The authors' recommendations about dose scheduling were not tested and are not part of this claim (no regimens on the site). Status single study: earlier studies cited by the authors point the same way but were not read.

statement: In people with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance treatment in high-income countries, periods out of treatment were associated with higher death rates than periods in treatment, with the highest rates in the first four weeks after leaving; three buprenorphine cohorts showed a similar but less certain pattern. A systematic review pooled 19 cohorts published 1974–2016 (18 methadone cohorts, 122,885 people, followed 1965–2010; 3 buprenorphine cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010; 11 in Europe or Israel, 4 in North America, 4 in Australia), counting time in and out of treatment for the same people (Sordo et al., 2017). With methadone, the pooled all-cause death rate was 11.3 per 1,000 person-years in treatment (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2) and 36.1 out of treatment (24.5 to 53.3), an unadjusted difference of 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1) and a ratio of 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86), in 16 cohorts; every cohort had a higher rate out of treatment (cohort rates 5.1 to 39.5 in treatment and 12.4 to 130.2 out). These pooled figures are random-effects averages across very different cohorts (I² 98%): in the three largest, recent register cohorts, which hold 83% of the person-years, the differences were 5.5 to 11.2 and the ratios 1.8 to 2.7, and adding up all deaths and person-years gives 7.1 against 16.4 (editors' calculations from the per-cohort figures). Overdose deaths with methadone (11 cohorts) were 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) in treatment against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4) out, a difference of 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4) and a ratio of 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96), higher out of treatment in every cohort. By time since starting or leaving methadone (five recent cohorts, after the review left out one cohort of people with HIV who inject; one cohort split at two weeks instead of four), the rate was 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) in the first four weeks of treatment against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) for the rest of treatment, a ratio of 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10) that was not statistically significant; and 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) for the rest of the time out of treatment, a difference of 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3) and a ratio of 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74), higher in the first period in each of the five cohorts; the review did not compare the weeks after leaving with time in treatment directly. The rise after leaving was seen in deaths from all causes: in the three methadone cohorts that gave overdose deaths by period, the overdose rate was 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) in the first four weeks after leaving against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1) later, from 20 overdose deaths in the first period, and in the two cohorts that gave both counts, 18 of the 79 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses (editors' count and calculation); the authors expect overdose deaths to be undercounted and note that deaths from suicide and injury are also more common in that period. With buprenorphine (3 cohorts; 96% of the deaths from Australian studies), the rate was 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) in treatment against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4) out (difference 5.2, −1.0 to 11.4; ratio 2.20, 1.34 to 3.61), 4.5 both in the first four weeks and in the rest of treatment, and 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) in the first four weeks after leaving against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9) later (two cohorts; difference 21.2, −5.9 to 48.2). All pooled estimates are unadjusted; in the cohorts that reported ratios adjusted for demographics, severity of drug use, treatment or illness (five methadone and one buprenorphine cohort for all causes), the ratios were unchanged or larger. But people leave and re-enter treatment for reasons that may themselves affect their risk; the review had no data on why people left or on tolerance or drug use after leaving, and its results do not separate people who finished a planned reduction from people who dropped out or were discharged; people lost to follow-up may be at higher risk; medicines obtained outside treatment were not captured; and people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or never treated were excluded. The authors suggest that loss of tolerance, assuming many people return to use, and the use of several substances may explain the rise after leaving. The discussion's statement that death rates were significantly lower with buprenorphine than with methadone has no test or estimate in the results. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Is it dangerous to stop methadone or buprenorphine? The weeks just after leaving treatment were the riskiest time in these studies. In 16 groups of people on methadone in high-income countries, about 11 in 1,000 died each year while in treatment, against about 36 in 1,000 a year after leaving, and every group had more deaths out of treatment; in the biggest recent groups the gap was smaller, about 6 or 7 a year against 12 to 18. In five groups that split time by weeks, deaths in the first 4 weeks after leaving methadone ran at about 32 a year per 1,000 people, against about 14 later on and about 6 after the first month in treatment. The first month on methadone may also carry more risk (about 11 a year per 1,000 people), but that could be chance. Buprenorphine had only three groups, mostly from one Australian study, with fewer deaths in treatment and a rise after leaving, less certainly. These studies counted everyone who left, for any reason, and could not say why people died: deaths counted as overdoses did not clearly rise after leaving, and nobody recorded tolerance or drug use. People who leave treatment may differ in ways that also affect their risk, so the studies cannot show how much stopping itself raises the risk.
population: People with opioid dependence who entered methadone maintenance (18 cohorts, 122,885 people, follow-up 1965–2010) or buprenorphine maintenance (3 cohorts, 15,831 people, 1990–2010) in 19 cohorts from high-income countries (11 Europe or Israel, 4 North America, 4 Australia); people in prison or recently released, in detoxification or other treatments, and never-treated people excluded
exposure: Periods out of methadone or buprenorphine maintenance treatment after leaving it, for any reason, with the first four weeks after leaving shown separately; and the first four weeks after starting treatment
comparator: Periods in treatment in the same cohorts (for the interval analyses, the rest of the time in treatment after the first four weeks, and the rest of the time out of treatment after the first four weeks); crude, unadjusted comparisons
outcome: Crude all-cause and overdose death rates per 1,000 person-years, from cohort records and population mortality registers
magnitude: Sordo et al. (2017), pooled crude rates per 1,000 person-years (bivariate random effects; unadjusted). Methadone, all causes (16 cohorts): in treatment 11.3 (95% CI 8.4 to 15.2), out 36.1 (24.5 to 53.3); difference 24.9 (13.6 to 36.1); ratio 3.20 (2.65 to 3.86); I² 98%; cohort rates in 5.1 to 39.5, out 12.4 to 130.2, higher out in all 16; leaving out one cohort at a time 10.6 to 11.9 in and 32.5 to 39.1 out. Editors' calculations from Fig 2: three largest cohorts (Degenhardt 2009, Evans 2015, Kimber 2015; 83% of person-years) differences 8.5, 11.2 and 5.5, ratios 2.5, 2.7 and 1.8; all deaths over all person-years 7.1 in against 16.4 out (ratio 2.3). Methadone, overdose (11 cohorts): 2.6 (2.1 to 3.3) against 12.7 (6.9 to 23.4); difference 10.0 (2.6 to 17.4); ratio 4.80 (2.90 to 7.96); I² 66% in and 97% out; higher out in all 11 (editors' reading of Fig 3). Methadone by interval (5 cohorts; Degenhardt 2009 split at two weeks): first four weeks in treatment 11.4 (5.8 to 22.4) against 5.8 (5.0 to 6.7) later in treatment, difference 5.6 (−2.4 to 13.6), ratio 1.97 (0.94 to 4.10); first four weeks after leaving 32.1 (19.1 to 53.9) against 13.5 (11.9 to 15.3) later out, difference 18.6 (2.9 to 34.3), ratio 2.38 (1.51 to 3.74); higher in the first period after leaving in each cohort (20.0 against 14.2 to 57.6 against 15.3). Trend analysis: fitted rate falling from 37.4 to 6.4 over the first four weeks of methadone treatment; 24.1 to 35.2 over the first two weeks after leaving, then declining (non-linearity P = 0.04). Overdose by interval, methadone (3 cohorts): in treatment 3.5 (1.3 to 9.5) against 2.0 (1.5 to 2.7); out 4.2 (1.8 to 9.9) against 3.4 (2.3 to 5.1); 20 overdose deaths in the first four weeks out (editors' count from Fig 6); in Kimber 2015 and Cousins 2016, 10 of 35 and 8 of 44 deaths in the first four weeks after leaving were counted as overdoses, 18 of 79 (editors' calculation from Figs 4 and 6, same person-years). Buprenorphine, all causes (3 cohorts): 4.3 (2.1 to 8.9) against 9.5 (3.9 to 23.4); difference 5.2 (−1.0 to 11.4); ratio 2.20 (1.34 to 3.61); by interval (2 cohorts) 4.5 in both treatment periods; first four weeks after leaving 32.0 (13.2 to 77.5) against 10.9 (8.5 to 13.9), difference 21.2 (−5.9 to 48.2), ratio 2.94 (1.34 to 6.46); overdose (1 cohort) 1.4 against 4.6, and 10.8 against 4.2 out of treatment by interval. Adjusted ratios (Table 4): all causes, methadone, unchanged in two cohorts and 15.5% to 35.5% larger in three; buprenorphine 16.8% larger in one; overdose unchanged in three methadone cohorts and 25.8% and 28.6% larger in two.

evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: the same people are compared in and out of treatment, but they leave and re-enter treatment non-randomly, so there could still be a large potential for confounding in crude comparisons, and confounders would need measuring at each exit and re-entry; dropouts are more likely among people at higher risk of death while out of treatment (informative censoring); the amount and direction of the resulting bias in the pooled estimates is hard to assess with the available information; studies were from high-income countries; overdose deaths when substitution medicines were obtained on illicit markets were not captured; a delayed record of leaving could misclassify deaths out of treatment as in treatment (making the estimates conservative); inconsistent overdose definitions and cause-of-death coding could misclassify deaths, which would tend to undercount overdose deaths.

evidence.extracted: The discussion states that comparing the medicines within the treatment period and within the period off treatment showed significantly lower mortality with buprenorphine than with methadone in both, and that the conclusions must remain tentative; no such test or estimate appears in the results, tables or figures, and it would compare 3 buprenorphine cohorts with 16 methadone cohorts from different countries and periods. Within-medicine comparisons showed a larger in-out difference with methadone than with buprenorphine.

risk_of_bias.note: Downgraded one level under METHODS §6.3 (a claim seen only through reviews: the cohorts were not read, so their risk of bias is not appraisable, and the one review is rated critically low by AMSTAR 2). The per-cohort data the review prints, the same direction in all 16 methadone cohorts, and adjusted ratios unchanged or larger in six cohorts are why it is not downgraded further.

inconsistency.note: Rates differ greatly between cohorts (I² 98% for all causes; 66% and 97% for overdose), but every cohort points the same way, and in each of the five cohorts with data by period the first weeks after leaving had a higher rate than later time out of treatment; the statement gives the range and the large-cohort figures.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: people who entered maintenance treatment in high-income countries and left it for any reason; the statement says that planned reductions are not separated from dropping out or discharge, that prison, detoxification and never-treated people were excluded, and that no low- or middle-income country is included.

imprecision.note: The methadone intervals exclude no difference (all causes 13.6 to 36.1; first four weeks after leaving 2.9 to 34.3). The start of methadone treatment and the buprenorphine figures are imprecise (intervals that include no difference, or resting mostly on one Australian cohort) and are worded as uncertain.

publication_bias.note: Some small-study effect for all-cause mortality (extended Egger P = 0.05), attributed by the authors to small cohorts of people with HIV who inject; none for overdose (P = 0.14). Not downgraded: the largest register cohorts show the same direction.

large_effect.note: Not applied (METHODS 6.3): the pooled ratios exceed 2 (3.20 all causes, 4.80 overdose) and adjusted ratios did not shrink, but adjustment was mostly for baseline factors, reasons for leaving that also raise the risk of death could bias away from no difference, and the largest register cohorts show ratios of 1.8 to 2.7.

grade.reasoning: Cohort studies are observational and start low; downgraded one level for risk of bias because the claim is seen only through one review, rated critically low, and the cohorts themselves were not read (METHODS §6.3, claims seen only through reviews): very low. Not downgraded further: the review prints each cohort's data, the direction holds in all 16 methadone cohorts for all causes and all 11 for overdose, and adjustment in six cohorts left the ratios unchanged or larger. The start of methadone treatment (not statistically significant), the buprenorphine figures (three cohorts, mostly one Australian study) and the overdose figures by period (three cohorts) are worded as uncertain and not rated separately. Whether treatment prevents deaths, or stopping causes them, is not claimed. Status: replicated (16 methadone cohorts from different countries and teams, same direction); one review read.
